beats.text: In 2019, Facebook was fined five billion dollars. [BEAT] The largest penalty in FTC history.
beats.why: FTC Chairman Joe Simons at the actual announcement podium — the most institutionally specific visual available for '$5B fine, largest in FTC history.' Grounds the viewer in the real event with government authority before any context is given.

beats.text: Let me show you what the math looks like when you put a face on it. Richard Grimshaw survived the Pinto fire. He grew up carrying scars that covered his body and a verdict that was supposed to change things — one hundred and twenty-five million dollars, reduced to three point five million. [PAUSE:1.0] The message was: we've done the math, and your pain has a price. [BEAT] Ford paid it and moved on. Yesenia Guitron called the ethics hotline and was fired for it. She never worked in banking again. [BEAT] Carrie Tolstedt, who built the quota system, kept fifty-seven million dollars.
beats.why: Narration opens the Reckoning chapter by putting a face on the math — and the first face is Grimshaw, the Pinto survivor. The crash test footage grounds the abstraction immediately: this is what the math cost a human body. play_then_mute lets the crash audio hit for 2-3 seconds before narrator takes over, preserving the visceral opening without competing with the character story.

beats.text: The Sackler name is still on a wing of the Guggenheim Museum in New York City. The Metropolitan Museum took theirs down after public outcry. [BEAT] The Guggenheim hasn't. You can walk into one of the most prestigious cultural institutions in the world, look up at the wall, and read the name of a family that earned their fortune from a drug that killed eight hundred thousand people. [BEAT] They kept thirteen billion. And they kept the wall.
beats.why: The narration explicitly names the Guggenheim Museum as the institution where the Sackler name remains on the wall. This is the only image in the pool showing the Guggenheim itself — placing it here makes the contrast between cultural prestige and eight hundred thousand opioid deaths viscerally concrete, not rhetorical.

beats.text: That's the formula. [BEAT] It even gets you a plaque.
beats.why: The narration delivers the chapter's thesis punchline — 'That's the formula. It even gets you a plaque.' Cutting to the Purdue Pharma building ties the abstraction of 'the formula' to the specific company whose naming rights on museum walls is the exemplar: crime industrialized, laundered into legacy.

beats.text: Elliana Esquivel is still making art in Charlotte. She pivoted to 3D — not because she chose to, but because the alternative was watching her style get reproduced for free. [BEAT] If the settlement arrives, her share might cover a month of rent. The model keeps running. Seventy-four percent of Facebook users still don't know the platform profiles them. The data harvested in 2014 was never deleted. [BEAT] The models built on it were refined. Chris Vialpondo is still in Seattle. Still working two jobs. [BEAT] The algorithm that raised his rent is still running. His fifty percent increase was not a market decision. It was a formula.
beats.why: The narration anchors Chris Vialpondo as 'still in Seattle, still working two jobs' — a Seattle residential neighborhood shot grounds his unresolved situation. The ordinary street-level calm contrasts with the algorithmic violence of RealPage still running beneath it, making the harm feel invisible and ongoing rather than historical.

beats.text: The Grush-Saunby memo put a dollar value on a human life in 1977. [BEAT] Two hundred thousand dollars. Purdue's settlement valued each opioid death at nine thousand. Facebook's fine valued each compromised user at fifty-seven dollars. The AI settlements value each stolen book at three thousand dollars. [BEAT] Elliana's illustrations? Not priced yet. Your Reddit posts? Your YouTube comments? Your blog from 2016?
beats.why: The narration recites the price assigned to each opioid death — $9,000 — Purdue's settlement figure. A Purdue/Sackler image locks that number to the company that set the price. Pairing it with the escalating text overlay transforms the stat sequence from abstraction into a verdict on a specific institution.
beats.sfx_motivation: The price-of-life escalation is the video's moral climax — a subterranean rumble signals to the viewer that the numbers they are hearing are not statistics but verdicts, building dread before the thesis lands.

beats.text: They'll get priced. [BEAT] And if fifty years of history tells you anything — [PAUSE:1.5] you won't like the number.
beats.why: The narration warns 'you won't like the number' — a vintage NYSE CRT monitor on the trading floor embodies the pricing system itself: the institution where everything, including human life and personal data, gets assigned a value. The retro monitor also echoes 'fifty years of history,' implying this mechanism predates the internet.

beats.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. [BEAT] It prices it.
beats.why: The video's thesis — 'The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.' — lands hardest against the literal entrance of the institution tasked with enforcement. The DOJ building becomes the ironic symbol: the law is the price list, and this is its headquarters. The institution's monumental scale makes the corruption feel structural, not incidental.
beats.text_overlay: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.
beats.sfx_motivation: The thesis statement is the single highest-stakes moment in the video — a sharp impact punctuates the revelation and gives the viewer a beat to absorb the line before the final two beats carry them out.

beats.text: The question was never whether they'd break the law.
beats.why: The narration reframes the entire documentary — 'The question was never whether they'd break the law.' Cutting to an empty boardroom table shows the audience where that question was literally never asked: not in courtrooms, but in rooms like this. The emptiness of the frame mirrors the moral vacuum the narration is describing.

beats.text: The question is what you're worth. Sources: NHTSA, Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co. (1981), FTC, SEC, DOJ, ProPublica, Copyright Alliance, CDC, European Data Protection Board, Washington State AG, WCNC Charlotte, Good Jobs First Violation Tracker, AlixPartners (2019).
beats.why: The final question — 'The question is what you're worth' — is addressed directly to the viewer. An aerial shot of an apartment complex positions the audience as the subject being surveyed from above: their rent, their data, their creative work, all awaiting a price. The overhead angle literalizes the power asymmetry — someone is always looking down and assigning numbers.
beats.text_overlay: The question is what you're worth.

beats.text: [BEAT] Eighty-seven million people's data — harvested, profiled, and sold to a political targeting firm without their knowledge.
beats.why: Zuckerberg in a CNN Breaking News chyron — directly anchors the '87 million people's data harvested' narration to the real person and the real scandal. The CNN BREAKING NEWS chyron signals this is documented fact, not allegation.

beats.text: [BEAT] And on the day the fine was announced, [PAUSE:1.0] Facebook's stock went up.
beats.why: The annotated Facebook stock chart from the exact day of the fine announcement is the evidence the narration references — the image IS the proof. No other visual can substitute; this is the specific chart showing the stock price rising on announcement day.
beats.sfx_motivation: The central thesis shock of the entire video — a $5B punishment made the company richer. This is the hook's payoff and demands a hard impact.

beats.text: The market added six billion dollars in value.
beats.why: Custom data graphic comparing the $5B fine against the $6B market gain — the only visual that shows both numbers simultaneously. Makes the absurdity concrete: the fine column is literally shorter than the gain column.

beats.text: Mark Zuckerberg personally gained one point one billion dollars in a single day.
beats.why: Custom data graphic showing Zuckerberg's personal $1.1B single-day gain — personalizes the structural absurdity to one human face. The person whose company was punished personally profited more than most people will earn in a thousand lifetimes.

beats.text: [BEAT] The punishment made the company richer than if the government had done nothing.
beats.why: FTC official on camera declaring 'Facebook betrayed the trust of its users' — playing this testimony mute while narration delivers 'the punishment made the company richer' creates maximum irony: the government declares its greatest victory while the target profits.

beats.text: How is that possible?
beats.why: Zuckerberg in a dark suit walking through a mob of photographers — a man surrounded but untouchable. Visually answers 'How is that possible?' by showing someone insulated from consequences, cameras swarming but never catching him.

beats.text: To understand, you need to go back to 1977. Because someone had to discover this trick.
beats.why: Grainy, low-resolution 1977-era footage still of the Pinto — the degraded image quality immediately signals the past. First visual anchor for '1977' and the Pinto case. Slower zoom signals deliberate deceleration before the story's historical anchor.

beats.text: [BEAT] And the discovery started with a car on fire.
beats.why: The Pinto mid-explosion crash test — a car literally on fire is the exact image the narration describes. Holds longer than a cut because the cold open's second act needs a sustained visceral image to cement viewer commitment before the formula is revealed.
beats.sfx_motivation: Hard impact on the explosion frame punctuates the cold open's final beat and signals the pivot into the historical story — the moment the formula was first discovered.

beats.text: In 1977, Ford knew the Pinto's fuel tank ruptured in rear-end collisions. They had the crash test data.
beats.why: Ford's actual cost-benefit analysis document — the 'crash test data' narration references internal paperwork, and this is that paperwork. A document claim requires a document visual. Showing the real memo makes the audience understand Ford didn't stumble into this: they wrote it down.

beats.text: [CHAPTER: THE FORMULA]
beats.why: Chapter card marks new section

beats.text: Two engineers wrote a cost-benefit analysis — an actual document, with actual numbers.
beats.why: The narration names an actual document with actual numbers — this is the Ford Pinto cost-benefit analysis itself. Show the document. Nothing else earns this moment.

beats.text: [BEAT] Fix every Pinto: one hundred and thirty-seven million dollars. Expected wrongful death payouts: forty-nine point five million.
beats.why: The narration reads the two numbers aloud — $137M fix, $49.5M deaths. The data viz graphic makes the cold math visible at the same moment the viewer hears it. Dual-channel hit: ear and eye simultaneously.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.5] They shipped the car.
beats.why: Three words: They shipped the car. The crash test explosion image lands like a verdict. Silence + fire = the most efficient visual punctuation available. The pause marker in the script demands we hold something devastating.
beats.sfx_motivation: Single hard hit on 'shipped' — the decision made real. One sound, then silence during the 1.5s pause.

beats.text: A thirteen-year-old boy named Richard Grimshaw was a passenger in a Pinto that was rear-ended in San Bernardino.
beats.why: Richard Grimshaw is introduced as a passenger in a Pinto. There is no image of Grimshaw — the car IS the character introduction. The viewer needs to see the specific vehicle that did this to a 13-year-old.

beats.text: The fuel tank ruptured. [BEAT] The driver burned to death. Richard survived — barely. [BEAT] Burned over his entire body.
beats.why: Narration: 'The fuel tank ruptured. The driver burned to death.' This still captures the Pinto mid-explosion — the exact physical event described. Using the real crash footage still, not generic fire, makes it specific and unerasable.
beats.sfx_motivation: Low rumble building through 'ruptured' — holds through the double BEAT pause before 'burned over his entire body.'

beats.text: Lost parts of his fingers. Lost his left ear. Years of skin grafts. [BEAT] A childhood replaced by hospital rooms.
beats.why: The narration catalogs physical damage: fingers, ear, skin grafts, hospital rooms. The post-explosion wreckage still holds that register — it's aftermath, ruin, what's left. Visual language matches the list of losses.

beats.text: The jury awarded one hundred and twenty-five million dollars in punitive damages — the largest in American history.
beats.why: The jury verdict moment — $125M, largest in American history. The gavel is the only visual that represents a court decision. It signals justice arrived. This beat needs the contrast: something that looks like accountability.
beats.text_overlay: $125M — largest punitive verdict in U.S. history

beats.text: The judge reduced it to three point five million. Ford was acquitted of criminal homicide.
beats.why: The judge cuts $125M to $3.5M and Ford walks on homicide. Return to the fire — same crime, different outcome. Visually rhyming the explosion with the acquittal forces the viewer to feel the injustice rather than just hear it.

beats.text: [BEAT] No executive went to prison. The fine was three point five million dollars. Ford kept selling cars.
beats.why: No executive in prison. $3.5M fine. Ford kept selling cars. Show the car — still on the road, still for sale, still normal. The Pinto as a product being sold is the proof that the system worked exactly as designed.

beats.text: No one went to prison. [BEAT] And somewhere in a boardroom, someone noticed something.
beats.why: The narration pivots from one story to the pattern: 'somewhere in a boardroom, someone noticed something.' The empty boardroom table is the exact visual — no faces, no names, just the room where the calculation lives. Abstract and ominous. Earns the chapter transition.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.5] The cost of getting caught was less than the cost of doing the right thing.
beats.why: The Ford Pinto cost-benefit memo IS the thesis statement made visual — 'cost of getting caught was less than cost of doing the right thing' is literally what that document calculated. The PAUSE:1.5 before this line demands the document that proves it.
beats.sfx_motivation: Lands on the thesis line — the central revelation of the entire video. Single heavy impact after the pause.

beats.text: That might have been an isolated scandal. A single bad company making a single bad calculation. [PAUSE:1.0] Except it wasn't.
beats.why: Narration pivots from 'isolated scandal' to 'except it wasn't' — this data image showing the pattern of fines across multiple companies is the visual proof that Ford was not anomalous. The PAUSE:1.0 before 'Except it wasn't' lands harder with a data chart behind it.

beats.text: In 2010, a twenty-four-year-old bank teller named Yesenia Guitron did something dangerous. [BEAT] She told the truth.
beats.why: Narration introduces Yesenia Guitron, a Wells Fargo bank teller. The branch storefront grounds the viewer in the institutional setting before the personal story — the yellow Wells Fargo sign is instantly recognizable and signals corporate power vs. individual.

beats.text: She'd watched her colleagues at Wells Fargo open accounts that customers never asked for — credit cards ordered to addresses that didn't exist, savings accounts funded by moving money between other accounts without permission.
beats.why: The A-roll narrator directly describes Wells Fargo tellers opening unauthorized accounts — the same act narration describes. Playing then muting this testimony anchors the claim in a credible third-party source before narration takes over the explanation.
beats.clip_audio_quote: for years, Wells Fargo employees created millions of unauthorized accounts on behalf of their customers

beats.text: She knew why they did it. There was a quota: every customer should have eight products.
beats.why: Narration explains the quota system — 'every customer should have eight products.' The extreme macro close-up of a credit card embossment makes the quota tangible and unsettling. Credit cards ARE the product being forced on customers who never asked for them.

beats.text: "Eight is Great." [BEAT] Miss the number and you get a warning. Miss it again and you get fired.
beats.why: A customer using a Wells Fargo ATM — someone being subjected to the system being described. 'Eight is Great. Miss the number and you get fired' needs a human victim in frame, not a logo. The back-turned posture adds isolation and anonymity.

beats.text: So the tellers cheated. Because the alternative was unemployment. Yesenia called the company's ethics hotline and reported the fraud.
beats.why: Narration says Yesenia 'called the ethics hotline and reported the fraud' — she is now a whistleblower. The A-roll establishes whistleblower credibility and institutional context right as she makes that choice. Play briefly then mute so narration continues uninterrupted.
beats.clip_audio_quote: Whistleblowers were responsible for exposing more fraud than internal audit departments

beats.text: [BEAT] Wells Fargo terminated her the same week. She never found steady work in banking again.
beats.why: Wells Fargo terminated her the same week — the betrayal lands harder with a Wells Fargo-specific image rather than a generic whistleblower still. The institutional brand in frame makes the corporation the subject of the sentence, not an abstraction.
beats.sfx_motivation: Punctuates 'terminated her the same week' — the retaliation is the second major revelation beat in this chapter.

beats.text: Her name went on an industry blacklist — a record that follows you like a scar.
beats.why: Narration describes an industry blacklist — 'a record that follows you like a scar.' The whistleblower commons image gives human scale to a systemic punishment mechanism. Stays on this visual as the emotional weight of her permanent exile settles.

beats.text: Three point five million fake accounts. Five thousand three hundred tellers fired for opening them.
beats.why: The scale numbers — 3.5 million fake accounts, 5,300 tellers fired — need a data visualization, not a building or face. This Wells Fargo accounts data image makes the numbers concrete and shareable. The text overlay turns it into a standalone graphic moment.

beats.text: And the woman who designed the quota — Carrie Tolstedt, head of Community Banking — kept fifty-seven million dollars and got zero prison time.
beats.why: Narration names Carrie Tolstedt keeping $57M with zero prison time — a Wells Fargo scandal still keeps the brand visible and the injustice concrete as the name and dollar figure land on screen
beats.sfx_motivation: Punctuates 'zero prison time' — the impunity reveal demands an audio hit

beats.text: She served her sentence at home. [BEAT] Ford's formula required a memo.
beats.why: Beat pivots hard from Wells Fargo to 'Ford's formula required a memo' — establishing the actual Pinto on screen the moment Ford is named anchors the callback and sets up the three-way escalation comparison

beats.text: Wells Fargo's didn't even require a decision — just a number and a threat.
beats.why: Narration says Wells Fargo only needed 'a number and a threat' — extreme close-up of embossed credit card represents the millions of unauthorized accounts opened under that quota, making the abstraction tactile

beats.text: Ford needed a document to do this. Wells Fargo only needed a quota. [PAUSE:1.5] The next company didn't need either.
beats.why: Narration draws an explicit three-way comparison — Ford needed a document, Wells Fargo needed a quota, the next company needed neither — a fine comparison data viz makes the escalating pattern visible and primes the Purdue reveal with dread

beats.text: It just needed a head start.
beats.why: Two-second beat — 'It just needed a head start' — Purdue branding on screen before the name is spoken lets viewers who know the story feel the dread, while new viewers get an ominous brand reveal

beats.text: Purdue Pharma saw the lawsuits coming a decade early and withdrew ten point seven billion dollars from the company before anyone could calculate the fine.
beats.why: Narration reveals Purdue withdrew $10.7B before anyone could calculate the fine — the opioid epidemic b-roll showing the human cost of the crisis makes the premeditation of that capital extraction morally overwhelming at the exact moment of disclosure

beats.text: [BEAT] Richard Sackler promised a, quote, blizzard of prescriptions at OxyContin's launch.
beats.why: Narration quotes Richard Sackler directly — 'blizzard of prescriptions' at OxyContin's launch — his face on screen as his own words are recited is the most damning editorial choice: it refuses to let the viewer treat this as institutional abstraction

beats.text: In Kermit, West Virginia — population four hundred — a single pharmacy received nine million opioid pills in two years.
beats.why: Narration delivers the Kermit, WV stat — 9 million pills to a population of 400 — an opioid crisis community image grounds the abstract number in the physical reality of a flooded town; the disproportion is visually self-evident

beats.text: [BEAT] The pharmacist went to prison. The Sacklers moved their money. [BEAT] More than eight hundred thousand Americans died.
beats.why: Narration lands 'eight hundred thousand Americans died' — the opioid death data visualization makes the body count a number the eye cannot escape; pairing it with 'the pharmacist went to prison / the Sacklers moved their money' forces the viewer to hold both facts simultaneously
beats.sfx_motivation: Audio punctuation on 'eight hundred thousand Americans died' — the scale of the number demands it

beats.text: The settlement: seven point four billion. The family's remaining fortune: thirteen billion. [PAUSE:1.5] Nine thousand dollars per death.
beats.why: Narration delivers the thesis ratio — $7.4B settlement, $13B family fortune remaining, $9,000 per death — holding the Sackler family image on screen as the per-death math lands refuses to let the viewer abstract it into policy; a human face owns the number

beats.text: Ford valued a life at two hundred thousand in 1977. The Sacklers got it down to nine thousand.
beats.why: The Pinto crash-test fire is the origin point of the cost-per-life formula. Holding on it as the narrator says '$200,000 in 1977' makes the explosion feel like an arithmetic problem — which is exactly the horror. This visual anchors the escalating price-per-life sequence that follows.
beats.sfx_motivation: Hard hit on 'nine thousand' — the number that makes $200K feel generous

beats.text: The fine is cheaper than the profit. Every time. [BEAT] Without exception.
beats.why: The fine-settle-repeat cycle graphic turns 'every time, without exception' from an assertion into a diagram. Showing the structural loop while the narrator names the loop makes the system feel engineered, not accidental — which is the entire thesis.

beats.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. [BEAT] It prices it.
beats.why: The thesis line of the entire video deserves the instrument of justice held at full stop. The gavel — symbol of legal authority — becomes the symbol of a pricing mechanism as the narrator reframes what it actually does. The irony IS the visual: hold it long, let the silence after 'prices it' breathe.
beats.text_overlay: THE LAW DOESN'T PREVENT CRIME. IT PRICES IT.

beats.text: And the price keeps dropping.
beats.why: A settlement check makes 'the price keeps dropping' literal — corporate crime is a check-writing exercise. The shorter the beat, the more concentrated the image needs to be. A close-up of someone signing away hundreds of millions lands harder than any abstract graphic on a 2-second cut.

beats.text: Since 2000, corporations have paid over one trillion dollars in fines and settlements in the United States alone.
beats.why: The data visualization IS the stat — narration and image are identical in content. The $1 trillion graphic exists precisely for this moment. Putting anything else on screen while the narrator says 'one trillion dollars' would create a mismatch between ear and eye.

beats.text: One hundred and twenty-seven companies have each paid more than a billion.
beats.why: The DOJ facade names the enforcement apparatus that extracted 127 individual billion-dollar penalties. Showing the institution gives the statistic institutional weight — these are not hypothetical fines, they are real buildings, real prosecutors, and still the price is always worth it.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.5] And here's the number that should end every argument about whether the system works: [BEAT] companies caught repeatedly pay smaller fines as a percentage of their revenue over time.
beats.why: This clip exists to validate viewer outrage before the reveal lands. A tech commentator reacting to corporations gaming fines with 'this is wild, this is some next-level BS' mirrors the emotional state the narrator is building toward. Cutting to a real person's disbelief during the 12-second setup makes the revelation at 'smaller' more earned.

beats.text: Not larger. Smaller. [BEAT] The more you violate, the better the deal gets.
beats.why: Wells Fargo is the canonical recidivist — fake accounts, mortgage fraud, auto insurance scams — with declining fine-to-revenue ratios across each settlement. The storefront is calm and ordinary, which makes 'the more you violate, the better the deal gets' land harder through visual contrast: the most repeat-offending bank in America looks like a bank.
beats.sfx_motivation: Single hard hit on 'smaller' — the word that inverts the audience's assumption about how punishment scales

beats.text: Each company added one feature to the original calculation. Ford added a memo. Wells Fargo added plausible deniability.
beats.why: Ford 'added a memo' — the cost-benefit analysis document is the defining artifact of the Ford chapter. This dark, grainy crash still represents the memo's consequence: a car that burned because a document said it should. The degraded image quality reads as archival and distant, which suits 'the original calculation' framing.

beats.text: Purdue added preemption. Facebook added scale.
beats.why: The annotated July 2019 Facebook stock chart — price going UP on the day of the $5B FTC fine — is the definitive proof that 'Facebook added scale.' The annotation is the editorial layer that turns a stock chart into an indictment. Scale means the fine is so small relative to the business that the market treats it as good news. No other image makes that argument with one frame.
beats.text_overlay: FACEBOOK STOCK WENT UP ON FINE DAY

beats.text: [BEAT] But every one of them had something in common — the damage, at least in theory, could be reversed.
beats.why: The 'settle cycle' diagram visually encapsulates the thesis that corporate damage was — in the old formula — theoretically reversible: fine, settle, repeat. Sets up the contrast about to be broken.

beats.text: Ford could recall the car. Wells Fargo could close the accounts. Purdue could stop making the pills.
beats.why: Narration lists Ford → Wells Fargo → Purdue as a closing triplet. Purdue is the most viscerally damaging of the three — ending on the opioid company image lands hardest and carries the cumulative weight of all three names.

beats.text: Then the formula met the internet. And the damage became permanent.
beats.why: 'The formula met the internet' is the pivot of the entire thesis — from physical recalls to permanent digital damage. Server racks are the visual symbol of that irreversible infrastructure. Muted stock footage lets the narration own this pivotal line.
beats.sfx_motivation: The pivot moment of the entire documentary — old formula meets the internet. The impact hit punctuates 'permanent.'

beats.text: Facebook was the bridge between the old formula and the new one.
beats.why: Facebook is named as the bridge between eras. The headquarters exterior grounds the company as an institution — the same establishing shot logic used for the DOJ or Ford in earlier chapters. Chapter THE DATA begins here.

beats.text: [CHAPTER: THE DATA]
beats.why: Chapter card marks new section

beats.text: In 2013, a Cambridge University researcher named Aleksandr Kogan built a personality quiz app.
beats.why: Narration introduces Aleksandr Kogan and the personality quiz — this custom data graphic for Cambridge Analytica shows exactly the data-harvesting mechanism being described, grounding the abstract 'app' in concrete evidence.

beats.text: Two hundred and seventy thousand people downloaded it.
beats.why: 270,000 downloads — a deceptively small, real number. The Cambridge Analytica wiki image shows the organization behind the quiz, making the viewer feel the gap between this modest app and what it would become. The mundane scale is the point.

beats.text: [BEAT] But Facebook's API — the system that connects apps to the platform — gave the quiz access to not just those users' data, but all of their friends' data too.
beats.why: The API loophole — quiz accessed not just 270K users but ALL their friends. This Cambridge Analytica voter data graphic shows the web of connected profiles, making the 'friends data too' mechanism visually undeniable.
beats.sfx_motivation: The API backdoor is the mechanism that makes everything else possible — this is where the story turns sinister. Slow tension riser under the 10-second beat.

beats.text: Every like, every post, every photo, every connection.
beats.why: 'Every like, every post, every photo, every connection' — the list belongs to Facebook. Cutting back to the building with the data accumulating in narration reinforces that this is Facebook's architecture enabling the harvest, not just Kogan's app.

beats.text: [BEAT] Two hundred and seventy thousand downloads became eighty-seven million people's data harvested in weeks.
beats.why: 87 million people — the number that broke the internet in 2018. The A-roll reporter explaining this scandal delivers the visual confirmation that this really happened. Running it muted under narration uses the credibility of broadcast journalism to validate the stat.

beats.text: Facebook knew this was possible.
beats.why: 'Facebook knew this was possible' — cut immediately to Zuckerberg walking into the Senate hearing surrounded by press. The image of accountability arriving proves the narration's accusation without a word. The crowd of cameras makes him look cornered.

beats.text: [BEAT] It was a feature, not a bug — they'd designed the API to be open because open APIs drive engagement, and engagement drives advertising revenue.
beats.why: Narration frames Facebook's open API as intentional corporate design — showing the Facebook campus/HQ exterior anchors this as a company decision made inside these walls, not an accident. Wide establishing shot lets the 'feature not a bug' thesis land against the benign facade of the company.

beats.text: In 2014, they quietly changed the rules. But they never enforced deletion of the data already taken.
beats.why: Different angle of Facebook HQ for visual freshness while narration pivots to the 2014 rule change — 'quietly changed' implies hidden action inside the institution. A cold exterior shot (different from beat 0) sustains the corporate-malfeasance frame without cutting away to unrelated footage.

beats.text: Cambridge Analytica used that data to build voter profiles so precise they could predict what would make you angry before you felt it.
beats.why: Narration is now describing Cambridge Analytica building precision voter profiles — this is the most specific available image of Cambridge Analytica's voter data operation. 'Predict what would make you angry before you felt it' demands a data/document visual, not a talking head.

beats.text: [BEAT] They were hired by the Trump campaign. They were hired by groups supporting Brexit.
beats.why: Narration names the Trump campaign and Brexit as Cambridge Analytica clients — this A-roll clip contains the exact sourced line 'Cambridge Analytica, which had worked on Donald Trump's presidential campaign, had improperly obtained…' Playing the clip's audio for 3s here gives the claim institutional weight (news broadcast confirmation) that narration alone cannot.
beats.clip_audio_quote: Cambridge Analytica, which had worked on Donald Trump's presidential campaign, had improperly obtained

beats.text: Eighty-seven million people's personalities — measured, modeled, and weaponized — for the price of a free quiz they never took.
beats.why: The '87 million people' stat is the chapter's quantitative gut-punch — showing it as a data graphic makes the number visceral and documentable rather than abstract. The data visualization also visually represents the 'measured and modeled' language in the narration.
beats.sfx_motivation: Scale of 87 million is the chapter's biggest revelation number — hard impact on 'weaponized' to snap the viewer.

beats.text: [BEAT] And most of them still don't know.
beats.why: Short hold (2.8s) on a static Cambridge Analytica image while the narrator says only 'And most of them still don't know' — the stillness IS the point. No motion, no text overlay, just the company name hanging in frame as the silence does the work.

beats.text: A 2019 Pew survey found that seventy-four percent of Facebook users didn't know the platform maintained a list of their interests and traits for ad targeting.
beats.why: Narration delivers the Pew 74% stat — Cambridge Analytica Wikimedia imagery keeps the chapter's visual throughline on the scandal while the text overlay carries the stat. Using a different Cambridge Analytica image maintains visual rhythm without repeating frames.

beats.text: They didn't know they'd been profiled. They didn't know their data had been sold.

beats.text: When a model trains on scraped data, that data dissolves into the model's parameters like sugar dissolved in water.
beats.why: AI training infrastructure actively running — not a finished product but a process in motion — mirrors the metaphor's active tense. Data dissolving into parameters is something happening right now, continuously, the way sugar doesn't stop dissolving once it enters the water. The machine that cannot be paused.

beats.text: You cannot un-dissolve it. You cannot identify which outputs came from which inputs.
beats.why: Common Crawl is the actual web-scraping dataset that feeds most major AI models — the literal inputs the narration says cannot be traced to outputs. Showing the source dataset as the narrator says 'you cannot identify which outputs came from which inputs' is direct evidence, not metaphor. The provenance problem made visible.

The face of the person whose sentence the model cannot identify lands at the exact moment the argument demands a human cost.

beats.text: That's not a company that got caught and feels chastened.
beats.why: RealPage's Irving, TX headquarters gives a face to the institution being described — 'a company that got caught and feels chastened' demands the physical building of the company, not a courtroom. The building looks unchanged, unbothered, still operational.

beats.text: [BEAT] That's a company that did the math and concluded — correctly, so far — that the system will let them continue.
beats.why: A NYSE floor trader in action — 'the system will let them continue' requires a visual of the financial system itself operating normally, as if nothing happened. The trader going about their day is the perfect embodiment of systemic indifference to corporate wrongdoing.

beats.text: Richard Grimshaw lost his fingers, his ear, and his childhood because Ford decided a hundred and thirty-seven million was too expensive.
beats.why: The actual 1977 Ford Pinto crash test explosion footage — while the narrator speaks Grimshaw's name and describes losing fingers, an ear, his childhood, viewers must see the fire that caused it. This is the only visual that makes that sentence land as human cost rather than abstraction.

beats.text: [BEAT] Chris Vialpondo works two jobs because an algorithm decided fifty percent more was the right number.
beats.why: An elderly man leaning on a high-rise apartment balcony railing — the Vialpondo callback ('works two jobs because an algorithm decided fifty percent more') needs a real human being in their apartment building, not a corporate graphic. This still shows the lived reality inside the buildings RealPage priced.

beats.text: [BEAT] The formula doesn't care whether it's a car or an apartment. It just runs the math.
beats.why: The overhead aerial shot of the NYSE trading floor reduces human beings to anonymous dots in a machine — 'the formula doesn't care whether it's a car or an apartment, it just runs the math' is the thesis crystallization. This impersonal bird's-eye view of the financial system IS that formula looking down at people.

beats.text: And sometimes, the price is zero.
beats.why: RealPage company imagery on 'the price is zero' — the $0 settlement after coordinating rent for 10 million apartments is the chapter's gut-punch payoff. Showing the company that paid nothing while viewers just heard what Grimshaw and Vialpondo paid makes the text overlay devastating.
beats.sfx_motivation: Chapter-closing revelation — the company that sued a state to keep its algorithm running paid zero dollars in fines. Hard impact on '$0' text appearance, then silence.

beats.text: Europe figured this out. [BEAT] Four percent of global revenue. Proportional. Automatic. No ceiling.
beats.why: Narration names Europe explicitly as the system that solved proportional fines — the EU Parliament building is the physical seat of GDPR legislation, grounding the abstract policy claim in a recognizable institution at the exact moment 'Europe figured this out' lands.

beats.text: [PAUSE:1.0] When the fine scales with the company, the formula breaks.
beats.why: The GDPR graphic is the mechanism that makes 'the formula breaks' concrete — it's the document that changed the math. Holding a GDPR-specific still while narration says 'the formula breaks' connects cause and effect without requiring narration to explain it.

beats.text: Facebook shrugged off a five-billion-dollar American fine and panicked over a European one. [BEAT] The tools exist.
beats.why: This clip shows the exact Meta-GDPR $1.3B fine that narration references — 'panicked over a European one.' Playing the news broadcast footage without audio while narrator draws the comparison between US $5B shrug and EU $1.3B panic gives the viewer the proof as they hear the thesis.

beats.text: Criminal liability for executives — not the tellers, the architects.
beats.why: Narration draws the tellers-vs-architects distinction using Wells Fargo as the implicit referent — Guitron was the teller who got fired, Tolstedt was the architect who kept $57M. A Wells Fargo branch exterior silently holds this tension: the institution that protected executives while punishing the people on the front lines.

beats.text: Disgorgement — hand back every dollar earned from the violation, not a negotiated fraction. [BEAT] The legal frameworks are built.
beats.why: Narration says 'the legal frameworks are built' — the DOJ aerial over Washington DC is the institutional symbol of those frameworks. The bird's-eye scale communicates that the infrastructure of justice genuinely exists; it is not absent, it is simply unused.

beats.text: The question has never been how. [PAUSE:1.5] The question is why.
beats.why: The rhetorical pivot — 'The question has never been how. The question is why.' — needs a visual that implies power and complicity without accusation. The 3D-rendered Capitol North Wing carries that implication: the seat of the people who could act and choose not to. The animated reconstruction feel adds an eerie, constructed quality that mirrors 'the answer is built into the system.'
beats.sfx_motivation: The 1.5s pause before 'The question is why' is the single most loaded moment in the chapter — an impact hit on the word 'why' marks it as a revelation, not just a rhetorical device.

beats.text: And the answer is the same math that runs everything else in this video.
beats.why: Narration says 'the same math that runs everything else in this video' — cutting to a trader gesturing on the NYSE floor closes the loop back to the financial system the entire documentary has circled. The gesture reads as explaining, calculating, justifying: the math being done in real time.

beats.text: [BEAT] The companies that benefit from the formula fund the campaigns, staff the advisory boards, draft the legislation.
beats.why: Narration explicitly names three mechanisms of regulatory capture: campaigns, advisory boards, legislation — all three originate in or are ratified by the Capitol. A wide aerial shot of the Capitol holds as the list builds, giving the viewer a single seat of power to attach all three mechanisms to.

beats.text: The fine stays small because the people who pay it set the ceiling.
beats.why: The thesis statement of the entire documentary — 'The fine stays small because the people who pay it set the ceiling' — lands over traders on the NYSE floor: the physical location of the people who pay the fines and fund the campaigns that set the ceiling. This is the definitive closing image: power, money, and the system as one.
